strapline: Ten defeated candidates close ranks on term limits; maize money starts flowing; ZESCO back in profit; two rulings at 11:00; and Burundi in Ndola for free

stories.title: 'Zambia does not belong to an individual': the ten candidates Hichilema beat in August sign one statement against removing presidential term limits
stories.excerpt: Harry Kalaba, Fred M'membe, Kelvin Bwalya Fube and seven other candidates from the 13 August election issued a joint statement in Lusaka on Thursday 12 November rejecting a proposal, attributed to the nominated youth MP Mwato Kabaso, to abolish presidential term limits. They cite the one-party years, Frederick Chiluba's failed third-term bid in 2001 and the 2024 ruling on Edgar Lungu's eligibility, and call on MPs of every party to defend the two-term rule. Zambia Monitor, the Daily Nation and the Zambian Observer carried the statement.

image.label: Ten signatures, one clause
image.caption: The candidates who lost to Hichilema in August say the presidency is an office of service, not an inheritance.

body: Ten of the people who stood against President Hakainde Hichilema in the general election of 13 August 2026 have put their names to a single statement opposing any move to remove the limit of two presidential terms. The statement, dated Thursday 12 November and issued in Lusaka, was carried in full by the Zambian Observer and reported by Zambia Monitor and the Daily Nation. It responds to a proposal that the three outlets attribute to Mwato Kabaso, a nominated Member of Parliament representing the youth.

The signatories, as listed on the statement, are Kelvin Bwalya Fube of Zambia Must Prosper, Given Chansa of the Movement for Economic Emancipation, Harry Kalaba of Citizens First, the independent Given Katuta, Howard Kunda of the Zambia Wake Up Party, Fred M'membe of the Socialist Party, Brian Mushimba of the Organised People's Party, Ackim Njobvu of the Democratic Union, Richwell Siamunene of the New Focus Party and Richard Silumbe of the Leadership Movement. Zambia Monitor gives two of the party names differently, listing Chansa under the Revamp Party and Njobvu under the Democratic Party.

The statement's central line, quoted by all three outlets, is that **"Zambia does not belong to an individual, a political party or an administration."** Zambia Monitor adds the candidates' description of the presidency as an office of service rather than an inheritance. The Daily Nation reports their warning that abolishing the limit could undermine Zambia's democracy and concentrate political power excessively.

According to the text published by the Zambian Observer, the candidates describe the Constitution as a social contract rather than the property of whoever holds office, and reject the argument that Zambia is short of capable leaders, pointing to the growth in educated professionals since independence. They recall the one-party period from 1973 to 1991, arguing that concentrated power damaged the economy and institutions, while acknowledging that commodity shocks also played a part. They cite the resistance to Frederick Chiluba's bid for a third term in 2001 as a democratic precedent, and the December 2024 court ruling that former President Edgar Lungu was not eligible to stand again as an example of the limit being enforced through the courts.

On the cost of elections, an argument sometimes made for longer or fewer terms, the statement accepts that polls are expensive but says the remedy is better electoral administration and public financial management, not fewer elections. The ten also say they are concerned that the proposal came from a young legislator, and urge young people not to confuse political ambition with democratic progress.

body.title: The six-point declaration, as published
items: Reject any proposal to abolish presidential term limits
Call on MPs of all parties to defend the principle of democratic succession
Ask young people, churches, civil society, traditional leaders and professional bodies to join the debate responsibly
Call for stronger independence for the Electoral Commission, the Judiciary, Parliament and other constitutional bodies
Urge the government to concentrate on jobs, education, health, infrastructure and poverty reduction
Encourage national dialogue and respect for differing views

body.text: What is not in the reports

body: None of the three reports records a response from Kabaso, from the UPND or from State House to the statement, and none says that any bill or motion to amend the term-limit provision has been tabled in the National Assembly. Zambia Monitor describes the Kabaso proposal as "reported", and the joint statement itself treats it as a proposal rather than a draft law. The candidates' statement is therefore a pre-emptive position, taken before any formal process has begun.

The ten were on opposite sides of each other in August, and the statement is the broadest common position the losing field has taken since the election. It is addressed as much to MPs as to the public: the second of its six points asks members of every party, including the governing one, to defend the succession rules they were elected under.

body.confirmed: That a joint statement dated 12 November 2026 opposing the removal of presidential term limits was issued in Lusaka in the names of ten candidates from the August election, and that it responds to a proposal attributed to nominated MP Mwato Kabaso: reported by Zambia Monitor, the Daily Nation and the Zambian Observer, the last of which published the full text.
body.unverified: Whether any formal amendment has been drafted or tabled; what Kabaso proposed in his own words and whether he has responded; the government's position; and the exact party names of two signatories, which Zambia Monitor and the published statement give differently.

stories.title: The maize money starts today: Moyo says farmers owed for 2025/26 deliveries to the FRA will be paid from Friday 13 November, drawing on K14.7 billion of the supplementary budget
stories.excerpt: Agriculture Minister Moses Moyo said in a statement on Thursday 12 November that payments to farmers who supplied maize to the Food Reserve Agency in the 2025/2026 marketing season and are still waiting would begin on Friday 13 November, following Parliament's approval of a K19.9 billion supplementary budget of which K14.7 billion is for the arrears. News Diggers and the Zambian Observer report the announcement; UPP president Saviour Chishimba says institutions that missed earlier timelines owe farmers an apology.

image.label: K14.7 billion, from Friday
image.caption: Farmers who delivered maize to the FRA months ago have a date for their money; the test is how fast it reaches them.

body: Farmers who delivered maize to the Food Reserve Agency during the 2025/2026 crop marketing season and have not yet been paid should start receiving their money on Friday 13 November, the Minister of Agriculture, Moses Moyo, said in a statement on Thursday reported by News Diggers. The payments follow Parliament's approval of a K19.9 billion supplementary budget, of which K14.7 billion is earmarked for settling what the government owes farmers.

According to News Diggers, Moyo thanked farmers for their patience and for their contribution to national food security and agricultural development. The Zambian Observer, which also reported that payments were to begin on Friday, described the announcement as a relief to farmers who had delivered grain and waited.

body.text: A date set from the top

body: The Zambian Observer carried a response from Saviour Chishimba, president of the United Progressive People, who thanked President Hakainde Hichilema for the announcement that payments would start on Friday 13 November. Chishimba's argument, as the outlet reports it, is that when the President gives a timeline the institutions beneath him must meet it, and that those who failed to do so on earlier occasions owe farmers an apology. He urged officials to act on presidential commitments rather than delay them, and closed by asking that every outstanding farmer be paid promptly.

The arithmetic of the supplementary budget is the backdrop. Of the K19.9 billion that Parliament approved, roughly three-quarters is for the maize bill owed to farmers who sold to the FRA. The first payments on Friday are the beginning of that process rather than the end of it: neither report gives a schedule for how quickly the K14.7 billion will be disbursed or how many farmers will be paid in the first tranche.

Two things will show whether the promise holds. The first is whether farmers in the districts furthest from Lusaka see money in their accounts in the coming days, rather than a further announcement. The second is whether the Treasury's release of the K14.7 billion is spread over weeks or compressed into the days before the planting season's input bills fall due. Chishimba's intervention, and the Zambian Observer's choice to frame the story around a presidential timeline, suggest the payments will be judged against the calendar as much as the total.

stories.title: From an operating loss to K6.3 billion after tax: Kapala hails ZESCO's turnaround on his first visit as Electricity Minister, and the utility's own report trims his K6.5 billion
stories.excerpt: Peter Kapala, the first holder of the new Electricity portfolio, visited ZESCO's head office on Wednesday 11 November and praised what a ministry statement called a K6.5 billion profit last year, crediting government reforms. ZESCO's 2025 Integrated Report records a group profit after tax of K6.3 billion on revenue of K32.7 billion, up from K30.8 billion, and an operating profit of K11.2 billion against an operating loss of K8.7 billion in 2024. Customers have grown from about 1.2 million in 2022 to about 1.5 million.

image.label: K6.3bn after tax, 2025
image.caption: ZESCO's 2025 accounts show a swing from an operating loss to profit; the minister's figure and the report's differ by K200 million.

body: The Minister of Electricity, Peter Kapala, used a familiarisation visit to ZESCO's head office on Wednesday 11 November to congratulate the utility on its return to profit. News Diggers, citing a statement from his ministry, reports that Kapala commended ZESCO for declaring a K6.5 billion profit last year after years of financial difficulty, and attributed the improvement to the government's policies and reforms in the electricity sector.

Green Building Africa, reporting the same visit, quotes Kapala calling the result "an encouraging improvement in the Corporation's financial performance". He met the ZESCO board, led by its chairperson Vickson Ncube, and the executive team under managing director Justin Loongo. Ncube said the utility had aligned its priorities with the Grow Zambia Agenda and its target of 10,000 megawatts of installed capacity by 2031; Loongo credited the better numbers to an expanded generation portfolio and cited the country's 1,000 MW solar milestone. ZESCO's customer base, the outlet reports, has grown from about 1.2 million in 2022 to about 1.5 million in 2026. Sitali Liyoko, the director for transmission, operations and trade, presented the roadmap to 10,000 MW.

ZESCO's own 2025 Integrated Report, covering the year to 31 December 2025, gives a slightly different headline figure from the one in the ministry's statement. The finance director's performance overview records a group profit after tax of K6.3 billion. Group revenue rose 6 per cent, from K30.8 billion in 2024 to K32.7 billion, and operating profit was K11.2 billion against an operating loss of K8.7 billion the year before. The report describes 2024 as a loss-making year without stating the net figure.

The K200 million gap between the minister's K6.5 billion and the report's K6.3 billion is not explained in either account; the report's figure is for the group, and the ministry statement does not say whether it refers to the company or the group, or to profit before or after tax. Both numbers point the same way, and the operating line is the more telling: a swing of almost K20 billion in a single year.

Kapala is the first holder of the newly established Ministry of Electricity, and Ncube congratulated him on the appointment, Green Building Africa reports. The visit was, in the utility's own framing as reported by Green Building Africa, a chance to brief the new minister on performance and to discuss expanding access and reliability for households, businesses and industry. The profit is being presented by the government as evidence that its reforms worked, and by ZESCO as the product of more generation. Neither report addresses the question that customers will ask first: whether a profitable utility will mean fewer load-shedding hours.

stories.title: 'No universal, one-size-fits-all' model: China's ambassador says Zambia's democracy should not be judged by a small number of outsiders, days after the EU's election dialogue
stories.excerpt: Speaking at a handover of computers, televisions and office equipment to the Nelly Mutti Crèche at the National Assembly on Wednesday 11 November, Ambassador Han Jing said Zambia's democratic future was for Zambians to decide and that each country may shape democracy to its circumstances. He praised the expanded Parliament for widening representation. News Diggers and the Zambian Observer report the remarks, which land as the government seeks to respond to the EU observers' final report before it is published.

image.label: Beijing's view of August
image.caption: A donation to Parliament became the occasion for China's ambassador to answer the EU's observers without naming them.

body: China's ambassador to Zambia, Han Jing, has said that the country's democratic future should be settled by its own people and not judged by what he called a small number of external actors. News Diggers reports that he made the remarks on Wednesday 11 November at a ceremony to hand over computers, televisions and other office equipment donated to the Nelly Mutti Crèche, items intended to improve efficiency at the National Assembly.

According to News Diggers, Han said there was no universal, one-size-fits-all model of democracy and that every country may shape its democratic path to fit its own circumstances. He also said the expanded composition of Parliament had strengthened the representation of groups that were previously under-represented. The Zambian Observer, reporting the same speech, adds that Han said Zambia's development should be understood in its own political, social and historical context, and frames his position as part of China's long-standing opposition to what it regards as external interference in other countries' political systems.

body.text: The audience he did not name

body: Neither report quotes Han naming any other country or organisation. The context is nonetheless clear from the week's news. On Monday 9 November the European External Action Service's director for Africa, Francesca Di Mauro, told the Zambia–EU Extraordinary Partnership Dialogue that no democracy is perfect but that electoral grievances should be handled "with transparency through a fair and impartial judicial process", and that the EU stood ready to support a national dialogue and reconciliation process, as News Diggers reported on 10 November. Foreign Affairs Minister Mulambo Haimbe asked at the same meeting for the government to be allowed to respond to the EU Election Observation Mission's final report before it is published.

The EU mission's chief observer, Michael McNamara, has also taken an interest in the court proceedings involving the opposition leaders Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, News Diggers noted in an editorial on Thursday, which recorded the UPND elections chairperson Likando Mufalali's warning to the Europeans against protecting criminals. The editorial's own position, in its headline, was that the EU report may not be accurate but that its concerns should be heard.

The sequence gives two of Zambia's major external partners visibly different readings of the August election within a single week: one urging transparent handling of grievances and offering to support reconciliation, the other saying the judgement belongs to Zambians alone. Han's remarks were made at a goodwill event rather than a press conference, and neither outlet reports a response from the government, the opposition or the EU delegation.

stories.title: Forms Five and Six return: Kamboni sets February 2027 for Zambia's first A-level intake, open to Grade 12 leavers of 2024 to 2026, with university entry from 2029
stories.excerpt: Education Minister Harry Kamboni announced on Wednesday 11 November that Advanced Level education will begin in February 2027 under the 2023 Zambia Education Curriculum Framework, adding a two-year stage after Ordinary Level. Candidates who sat Grade 12 in 2024, 2025 or 2026 may apply for the first intake, taking up to four subjects from approved combinations across twelve pathways; placement runs from 25 to 31 December. The Daily Nation, News Diggers and the Zambian Observer report the briefing.

image.label: February 2027
image.caption: A two-year advanced stage is added above Grade 12; the first cohort could reach university in 2029.

body: Zambia will introduce Advanced Level secondary education in February 2027, the Minister of Education, Harry Kamboni, announced at a media briefing on Wednesday 11 November. The reform, reported by the Daily Nation, News Diggers and the Zambian Observer, adds a two-year advanced stage under the 2023 Zambia Education Curriculum Framework: Forms One to Four will lead to an Ordinary Level qualification, and Forms Five and Six to Advanced Level.

For the first intake, eligibility extends to candidates who completed their Grade 12 examinations in 2024, 2025 and 2026, subject to prescribed requirements and approved subject combinations, News Diggers reports. Kamboni said eligible learners would be placed between 25 and 31 December 2026. He described the introduction as "an important milestone in implementing the 2023 Zambia Education Curriculum Framework".

The Daily Nation lists the subject pathways on offer: Natural Sciences, Agricultural Science, Computer Science, Business Studies, Design and Technology, Social Sciences and Languages, Performing and Creative Arts, Physical Education and Sports, Hospitality Management, Travel and Tourism, Textile Design and Technology, and Nutrition and Food Technology. Students may register for a maximum of four A-level subjects chosen from approved combinations. From 2029, A-level holders will be able to enter suitably structured degree programmes, subject to each institution's admission criteria.

Kamboni was joined at the briefing by the Permanent Secretary for Administration, Noriana Muneku, the Permanent Secretary for Educational Services, Dr Kelvin Mambwe, and the Executive Director of the Examinations Council of Zambia, Dr Michael Chilala, according to the Daily Nation. The minister said the reform would prepare young people for a modern, competitive and knowledge-driven economy, broaden learners' choices and build skills for national development.

The three reports describe the structure and the timetable but not the resourcing: how many schools will offer Forms Five and Six from February, how many teachers will be deployed to them, and what the fees or bursary arrangements will be. The pathways list implies specialist facilities, from laboratories to kitchens and workshops, that not every secondary school has. Those details, and the mechanics of placement over the last week of December, are the ones parents of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 Grade 12 cohorts will be waiting for.

stories.title: A plea on 24 November and a ruling at 11:00 today: Mundubile and Zulu face the sedition charges without counsel, as the High Court rules on their account of the UN refuge
stories.excerpt: Lusaka Resident Magistrate Webster Milumbe refused an adjournment on Wednesday 11 November and ordered Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu to take plea on two counts of seditious practices; when Bonaventure Mutale, Sakwiba Sikota and Chifumu Banda said they had no instructions, he let them withdraw and set 24 November for a possible plea. In the treason bail case, the High Court rules on Friday 13 November at 11:00 on the State's bid to strike five paragraphs and a video from the applicants' affidavit, then hears the bail plea itself.

image.label: 24 November, 11:00 today
image.caption: Two courts, two calendars: a plea in the sedition case in eleven days, and a ruling in the treason bail case this morning.

body: Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu will be asked to plead to two counts of seditious practices on Tuesday 24 November, after a hearing on Wednesday 11 November in which their lawyers withdrew and the two politicians, both lawyers by training, addressed the Lusaka Magistrates' Court themselves. Zambia Monitor, News Diggers and the Times of Zambia report the hearing before Resident Magistrate Webster Milumbe, in a case transferred to Lusaka from Solwezi.

According to Zambia Monitor, the magistrate initially insisted that the accused take plea and rejected a defence application for an adjournment, saying counsel had had enough time to obtain instructions. The Director of Public Prosecutions, Gilbert Phiri, opposed the adjournment, News Diggers reports, on the ground that the accused were not ready to plead. Senior counsel Bonaventure Mutale and Sakwiba Sikota told the court they could not proceed without instructions from their clients and asked to withdraw, which the magistrate allowed; the Times of Zambia also names Chifumu Banda among the lawyers who left.

body.text: Why the accused would not plead

body: Zulu told the court, as Zambia Monitor reports it, that the two had understood they were coming to Lusaka for High Court proceedings, not to take plea in the transferred matter, and that pleading before preliminary issues were resolved could undermine the applications they intend to make, including whether the charges disclose an offence at all. The accused said they had difficulty preparing from detention without phones or laptops. Zulu asked for 14 days; the magistrate granted seven and indicated 24 November as a possible plea date, adjourning, in the Times of Zambia's account, "in the interest of justice".

The Times of Zambia sets out the two counts: that Mundubile allegedly called on the Electoral Commission of Zambia to release results and declare the winner of the 13 August election on the strength of a parallel vote tabulation, and that Zulu allegedly announced on Facebook that Mundubile would address the nation at a scheduled time. A contributor's account in the Zambian Observer says both men deny the charges and that they invoked their right to counsel under Article 18 of the Constitution before the plea was deferred.

body.text: Five paragraphs and a flash disk

body: In the separate constitutional bail application by Mundubile, Zulu and 16 co-accused in the treason case, the Lusaka High Court has reserved its ruling on the State's objection to Friday 13 November at 11:00, with the substantive bail arguments to follow. The Zambian Observer, carrying a Kalemba report, says the State wants five paragraphs struck from the applicants' affidavit, paragraphs that explain why Mundubile and Zulu sought refuge at a United Nations facility before surrendering to police. Chief State Advocate Chali Hambayi argued the paragraphs raised matters not previously pleaded: "If we had not raised that objection, those matters would have gone on to the court without us having an opportunity to respond to them."

body.text: They did not expect them to just say we are not a flight risk, they needed to explain how they are not a flight risk.
body.attribution: Milner Katolo, defence lawyer, speaking after the Lusaka High Court hearing on Wednesday 11 November, as reported by Kalemba via the Zambian Observer

body: Katolo argued that going to the UN facility after alleged shootings at the two men's homes and the death of Mutotwe Kafwaya was driven by fear for their lives and does not make them flight risks, and that the paragraphs are a clarification rather than new evidence. The State had itself cited the UN stay as a reason to oppose bail, he said. The applicants are asking for unconditional release or bail on reasonable conditions, arguing that prolonged detention without trial breaches their constitutional rights.

body.confirmed: That the magistrate refused an adjournment, allowed the defence lawyers to withdraw and set 24 November for a possible plea (Zambia Monitor, News Diggers, Times of Zambia); that the High Court will rule at 11:00 on Friday 13 November on the State's objection to parts of the bail affidavit before hearing the bail application (Zambian Observer, carrying Kalemba).
body.unverified: Whether Mundubile and Zulu will have new counsel by 24 November; how the High Court will rule on the five paragraphs and the video; and the outcome of the bail application itself. The charges are allegations; both men deny them and no plea has been taken.

stories.title: Bonds of K538,000 and two Toyotas: the ACC charges a Lusaka Archdiocese priest with concealing K1.5 million it links to a former Community Development officer's K5.6 million case
stories.excerpt: The Anti-Corruption Commission said on Thursday 12 November that it had arrested and charged Fr Titus Malama Sande, 45, with four counts of possessing and concealing property reasonably suspected to be proceeds of crime: bonds worth K538,000 at a bank, and a Toyota Hilux and Toyota Dyna worth about K1 million registered in his name but, the ACC alleges, acquired by Veronica Chisanga Kabwe. He has been released on bond and is to appear in court. News Diggers, Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer report the statement.

image.label: Four counts, K1.5 million
image.caption: The ACC says the vehicles and bonds trace back to a case it opened last month; the priest is yet to answer in court.

body: The Anti-Corruption Commission has arrested and charged a Catholic priest of the Lusaka Archdiocese with four counts of possessing and concealing property worth about K1.5 million that it suspects to be proceeds of crime. News Diggers, Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer all report the statement issued on Thursday 12 November by the commission's head of corporate communications, Joseph Mwenya, which names the priest as Fr Titus Malama Sande, 45, of 15 Miles in the Chikumbi area of Chibombo District.

The charges are brought under Section 71(1) of the Forfeiture of Proceeds of Crime Act No. 19 of 2010 and relate to dates unknown between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2025 in Lusaka District, allegedly jointly with other persons unknown, according to Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer. Counts one and two concern bonds valued at K538,000 held at a bank, which the reports do not name. Counts three and four concern a Toyota Hilux and a Toyota Dyna light truck with a combined value of about K1 million.

body.text: The link to an earlier case

body: The ACC's case, as the three outlets report it, is that the two vehicles were registered in the priest's name although he knew they had been acquired by Veronica Chisanga Kabwe, a former executive officer at the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services. Kabwe was arrested last month together with Chimangeni Banda, a senior news editor at the Zambia News and Information Services, for allegedly possessing and concealing property worth K5.6 million. Mwenya said Thursday's arrest was linked to that case.

Sande has been released on bond and is expected to appear in court soon; no date has been given. None of the three reports carries a response from the priest or from the Archdiocese of Lusaka, and the charges are allegations that have yet to be tested. The ACC used the statement to urge the public to avoid corrupt practices and to report suspected corruption, saying that concealing proceeds of crime would not be tolerated regardless of status.

body.confirmed: That the ACC arrested and charged Fr Titus Malama Sande on four counts under Section 71(1) of the Forfeiture of Proceeds of Crime Act, relating to K538,000 in bonds and two vehicles, and released him on bond, as stated by the ACC and reported by News Diggers, Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer; that the ACC links the case to the October arrests of Veronica Chisanga Kabwe and Chimangeni Banda.
body.unverified: Every element of the allegation, including who paid for the vehicles and bonds and whether the priest knew their provenance; his response and the Archdiocese's; the court date; and the outcome of the K5.6 million case against Kabwe and Banda, which has also not been tried.

stories.title: Fifty-six deaths and 2,658 suspected cases: cholera has added a thousand cases since late October, as the WHO offers help on water and the water minister calls in the NGOs
stories.excerpt: News Diggers reports Zambia National Public Health Institute figures of 98 new suspected cases and one death in 24 hours, taking the outbreak to 2,658 suspected cases, 351 confirmed and 56 deaths, with 138 people in hospital; on 28 October the toll stood at 1,622 cases and 30 deaths. WHO representative Dr Clement Lasuba told the Local Government ministry on Wednesday that most of Zambia's diseases are preventable and need more than one ministry; Elisha Matambo told the 65-member NGO WASH Forum that universal access needs all hands.

image.label: 56 deaths, 2,658 cases
image.caption: The toll has almost doubled in a fortnight; the ministries responsible for water and local government are now being drawn in.

body: Zambia's cholera outbreak has now killed 56 people, according to Zambia National Public Health Institute figures reported by News Diggers on Thursday 12 November. The institute recorded 98 new suspected cases and one death in the previous 24 hours, with four cases laboratory-confirmed, taking the cumulative count to 2,658 suspected cases, 351 confirmed and 56 deaths. Some 138 patients were in hospital and 2,464 had recovered and been discharged.

The figures mark a sharp acceleration. On 30 October, News Diggers reported that the Health Minister, Professor Roma Chilengi, had told Parliament of 1,622 cases and 30 deaths as of 28 October, across 20 districts in six provinces, with Lusaka Province accounting for 1,090 cases and 16 of the deaths occurring in communities before patients reached a health facility. In a little over two weeks the case count has risen by more than a thousand and the death toll has almost doubled.

News Diggers also reports that the Copperbelt provincial health director, Dr Charles Mwinuna, has disputed reports that two people died of suspected cholera in Mpongwe, saying the province had recorded only three cholera cases. None of the reports gives a district breakdown of the latest national figures.

The World Health Organization's representative in Zambia, Dr Clement Lasuba, paid a courtesy call on the Ministry of Local Government on Wednesday 11 November and said the WHO was ready to work with the government to strengthen water and sanitation interventions against cholera, News Diggers reports. Most diseases in Zambia are preventable, he said, and dealing with them needs many stakeholders, because health challenges begin at household and community level before they become district, provincial and national concerns.

body.text: When we think of health primarily, we think it is the responsibility of the Ministry of Health.
body.attribution: Dr Clement Lasuba, WHO Representative to Zambia, at the Ministry of Local Government on Wednesday 11 November, as reported by News Diggers

body: On the same day, the Times of Zambia reports, the Minister of Water Development and Sanitation, Elisha Matambo, received the national coordinator of the NGO WASH Forum, which has 65 member organisations working in all ten provinces, at his Lusaka office. He said partnerships with civil society were key to expanding access to water, sanitation and hygiene services, and that universal access requires the "collective efforts of Government, cooperating partners, civil society organisations", together with the private sector and communities.

Taken together, the three reports show the response widening from treatment centres to the ministries that control water supply, drainage and local markets, the ground on which cholera is won or lost. What none of them yet gives is a fresh count of affected districts, or a date by which the institute expects the daily case numbers to turn.

WHO pledges support towards cholera eradication

stories.title: Free entry at Levy Mwanawasa and 'an element of madness': Zambia meet Burundi at 15:00 today with the President's tickets in the stands and four forwards missing
stories.excerpt: Kick-off in Ndola is at 15:00 CAT on Friday 13 November. The Zambian Observer reports that Sports Minister Likando Mufalali announced the President had bought all the tickets so that supporters enter free, four days after Hakainde Hichilema told FAZ he would buy 'a lot of tickets'. George Lwandamina asked his players for 'an element of madness'; Fashion Sakala said the replacements for Daka, Lameck Banda, Gamphani Lungu and Kingstone Mutandwa are ready. Algeria lead Group I on four points, Togo and Zambia have three, Burundi one.

image.label: Zambia v Burundi, 15:00
image.caption: A full stadium at no charge, a coach asking for madness and a return leg in Bujumbura next week.

body: Zambia play Burundi in their third 2027 Africa Cup of Nations Group I qualifier at the Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Friday 13 November, with kick-off at 15:00 CAT, and supporters will not pay to get in. The Zambian Observer reports that the Minister of Youth and Sports, Likando Mufalali, announced that President Hakainde Hichilema had bought all the tickets for the match so that fans could watch free of charge. The announcement follows the President's pledge on Monday 9 November, reported by ZamFoot, when he answered an invitation from FAZ president Keith Mweemba to attend as the association's patron: "We are going to buy tickets for the game in Ndola. A lot of tickets." ZamFoot reported him saying the support would continue beyond this fixture and that ticket proceeds would give FAZ a margin.

The coach, George Lwandamina, told Thursday's pre-match press conference in Ndola that Burundi would be difficult but that his side was prepared, ZamFoot reports: "It won't be an easy game, but what I have asked of my players is the element of madness that will give us the edge." Patson Daka, Lameck Banda, Gamphani Lungu and Kingstone Mutandwa are injured, and Edward Chilufya, Prince Mumba and Derrick Bulaya have been called up in their place. Lwandamina, the former ZESCO United coach, played down the absences and said the squad had enough cover.

Captain Fashion Sakala, the Al-Fayha forward, said a passionate home crowd could be decisive and asked the media to help build the excitement. "It is a big advantage for us, definitely having you guys," he told reporters, according to ZamFoot, adding that fans at home were like extra players on the field and that he felt very confident. He welcomed the President's ticket pledge as a sign that sponsorship starts from the top. News Diggers, reporting the same briefing from Ndola, quotes him on the injuries: "To be honest, I think we are very much ready." Lwandamina warned that Burundi should not be underestimated even though they are the group's underdogs.

Burundi arrived in Ndola on Tuesday 10 November and had held two training sessions by Thursday, when they were due to train at the Levy Mwanawasa pitch itself, ZamFoot reports. The two sides meet again in Bujumbura next week on matchday four.

After two matchdays Algeria lead Group I on four points, Togo and Zambia have three each and Burundi have one, according to ZamFoot, which lists Zambia third, level on points with Togo. A win on Friday would put Zambia on six points before Algeria and Togo complete their own back-to-back fixtures. Lusaka Brief will report the result and the return leg in Bujumbura in the editions that follow; this page was published before kick-off.

stories.title: A 32-team knockout and a first women's national cup, backed by KCM's US$1.6 million; and in Philadelphia tonight, Patrick Chinyemba turns professional against an unbeaten American
stories.excerpt: FAZ and Konkola Copper Mines launched the KCM–ZFA Men's and Women's Cups at KCM's headquarters in Chingola on Thursday 12 November: 32 teams from the Super League, the National League and the provinces over 31 matches in five rounds, and the first dedicated national cup for women, ZamFoot reports. KCM's deputy chief executive Satish Kumar put the company's 2026 commitment to Zambian football at US$1.6 million. In the United States, two-time Olympian Patrick 'Baddo' Chinyemba makes his professional debut on Friday 13 November against Santiago Vazquez.

image.label: Two new cups, one sponsor
image.caption: A knockout for clubs below the top flight, a first national cup for women, and a Zambian bantamweight's first paid fight.

body: The Football Association of Zambia and Konkola Copper Mines have launched two new national knockout competitions, the KCM–ZFA Men's Cup and the KCM–ZFA Women's Cup, at a ceremony at KCM's headquarters in Chingola on Thursday 12 November, ZamFoot reports. The inaugural men's edition for 2026 will bring together 32 teams drawn from the MTN Super League, the National League and the provincial divisions, playing 31 matches over five rounds. The women's competition is described as the first dedicated national cup for women's football in Zambia.

FAZ president Keith Mweemba called the launch an important milestone and said the competitions were part of his plan to widen opportunities for clubs and to fill a gap in the women's domestic calendar. He acknowledged that the first edition would have to fit within the transitional football calendar, and said the aim was to make both tournaments permanent fixtures. Satish Kumar, KCM's deputy chief executive, said the company had committed US$1.6 million to Zambian football in 2026, covering its partnership with FAZ and support for the Chipolopolo and the Copper Queens, and described the cups as a grassroots investment that gives players in the lower divisions and community leagues a route upwards.

Patrick "Baddo" Chinyemba, who boxed for Zambia at two Olympic Games, fights as a professional for the first time on Friday 13 November at the 2300 Arena in Philadelphia, News Diggers reports. He meets the undefeated American Santiago Vazquez over six rounds at bantamweight on Red Owl Boxing's BOXFEST XXII card. Chinyemba, who intends to use the Philly Shell defence associated with the city he is fighting in, closed his amateur career with a bronze medal for Zambia at the IBA World Boxing Championships in Dubai on 11 December 2025. "Two days to go until my professional debut," he said in remarks carried by News Diggers on Thursday.

The two stories sit at opposite ends of Zambian sport's funding problem. The KCM money is a mining company putting a sum it can name into a competition that gives clubs outside the top flight a reason to exist beyond their provincial leagues, and gives women's teams a national trophy to play for; whether the 32 teams can afford to travel for five rounds is the question the first edition will answer. Chinyemba's debut is a Zambian athlete taking his career to the market where the purses are, with no national structure behind him once the amateur medals are won. Both results, the cup draw and the fight, belong to the weekend's reporting.

analysis.title: A statement against a proposal that does not yet exist on paper
analysis.body: The ten candidates have taken a position before there is anything formal to oppose. All three outlets attribute the term-limit idea to a nominated youth MP, and none reports a bill, a motion or a government endorsement. That timing is the point: the signatories want the two-term rule defended as a principle before any text appears, so that a future proposal arrives into a settled argument rather than an open one. The strongest case for their side is history, which they make themselves: the one-party years and the 2001 third-term fight. The strongest case on the other side, which the statement acknowledges and tries to answer, is cost and continuity, the argument that frequent elections are expensive and that a term limit can remove a leader voters still want. What is unknown is whether anyone in the governing party intends to carry the idea further. The things to watch are a response from Kabaso or from State House, any notice of a constitutional amendment bill, and whether UPND MPs answer the statement's direct appeal to them.

analysis.title: Why the first week of maize payments matters more than the total
analysis.body: The K14.7 billion for farmers is three-quarters of the supplementary budget Parliament approved, and the government has now attached a date to it. The number that will decide how the policy is judged, though, is not the total but the pace. Farmers delivered maize to the FRA months ago on a promise of payment, and the inputs for the coming season are being bought now. For any farmer who financed the last season on credit, a fortnight's difference in when the money lands changes whether it goes into the ground or into servicing debt. The Treasury's side of the argument is that it had to find the money through a supplementary budget, and that releasing K14.7 billion in days rather than weeks has consequences for liquidity and for the kwacha. What remains unknown is the disbursement schedule: how many farmers are paid on Friday, in which provinces, and whether the oldest deliveries are settled first. If the payments run smoothly, the political cost of the delay fades. If they stall again, Saviour Chishimba's demand for an apology will be the mildest reaction.

analysis.title: Eleven o'clock: what the High Court's ruling on five paragraphs will settle
analysis.body: The objection the three-judge panel rules on this morning looks small. The State wants five paragraphs and a video removed from the affidavit of the 18 applicants; the defence says the material explains why two of them took refuge at a UN facility and answers the flight-risk argument the State itself raised. Underneath is a question that will shape every constitutional bail application after this one: whether an applicant may answer the State's objections in a reply affidavit, or must anticipate them in the original filing. The State's position, put by Chief State Advocate Chali Hambayi, is procedural fairness, that it cannot respond to matters pleaded late. The defence's, put by Milner Katolo, is that a clarification is not new evidence and that the court should weigh it rather than exclude it. Either way, the substantive bail hearing follows the ruling, and the sedition plea in the magistrates' court is set for 24 November. What is unknown is whether Mundubile and Zulu will have new lawyers by then, and whether the High Court's reasoning on the affidavit will be applied to the sedition file too.
